title: World's Lightest Solid!
beats: Lightest solid, 99.8% air; poses four questions (why invented, how made, why insulates, uses)
Chocolate bunny on glass vs on aerogel under Bunsen burner, thermal camera; bunny on glass melts fast and dish cracks
Kistler 1931 bet about jellies: can you remove the liquid without collapsing the solid
Jelly as mostly liquid in a 1% solid skeleton with nano pores
Simply evaporating pulls on molecules and crumples the skeleton
Two fixes: swap liquid by washing, then go supercritical so no liquid/gas pull
Left-behind skeleton with gas in pores is aerogel; cut back to still-running burner test
Hands-on: wet silica gel 97% alcohol, crumbly; swap to liquid CO2 (why CO2: non-flammable, low critical temp)
Hairdryer heats CO2 to critical point; surface blurs and vanishes, sped up
Blue tint = Rayleigh scattering, 1/wavelength^4 stated after the sight; looks yellow against sky
Held to blue sky it is a portable sunset
Not same as air: better insulator because pores smaller than mean free path (Knudsen effect)
Mars rovers insulation; Stardust comet dust capture as porous brake
Antarctic skyscraper joke; costs, fragility, hydrophilic demo; trilogy teaser

theory: The video keeps a live experiment running while the mechanism is explained in pieces, so the payoff of each idea is visible in the demo, not asserted. Each mechanism step (why shrinks, why supercritical, why scattering, why Knudsen) answers a concrete thing the viewer just saw or touched.
velocity: Scene builder: support a long-running 'demo thread' scene that the explanation cuts away from and returns to, with state preserved
Orchestrator: when a naive method fails, show the failure first (evaporate gel collapses), then introduce the fix as a repair
Voice: delay the formula until after the surprising visual; use formula as a label not a source
Ghost hands: pointing at the bunny edge where melting starts at 5:49 is the model for guiding attention to the evidence
